blocks.title: Make responsibilities and types visible
paragraphs: Readable code exposes the contract it implements. Extract repeated logic for a clear responsibility, parse strings according to a stated grammar, and use generics to keep type mistakes at compile time.

blocks.title: Refactor while preserving behavior
paragraphs: If one method reads input, decodes records, filters them and prints a report, give each stage a name and a focused contract. Keep parsing independent of console input so a small String or Reader can be tested without a terminal.

Prefer names that reveal units and intent, eliminate duplicated rules, and group parameters only when they represent one real concept. Keep regression tests running as structure changes. A short method with a misleading name is not automatically good; line counts and coverage percentages are signals, not proofs of quality.

blocks.title: Make the record grammar explicit
paragraphs: This authored mini-format is label|count, with exactly two fields, a nonblank label and a strictly positive integer. split uses a regular expression: the vertical bar is escaped. The negative limit retains trailing empty fields so "oak|" remains visibly malformed.

Trim fields deliberately, check their count before indexing, then convert the numeric token and enforce its domain. String methods return values; they do not mutate an existing String. Scanner token methods and nextLine consume different units, so understand what remains after reading a token.

blocks.title: A type argument is a compile-time promise
paragraphs: List<String> accepts String elements and returns String from get. List<Integer> uses the wrapper type; List<int> is invalid. A Box<T> can use T consistently in its field, setter and getter without requiring casts from its clients.

Generics are invariant: List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>. Otherwise an Object could be inserted through the wider view and later read as String. A bound such as T extends Number limits allowed type arguments; it does not mean every T is interchangeable.

Type erasure means List<String> and List<Integer> do not become distinct specialized runtime classes. This does not remove ordinary runtime object types or compiler-inserted casts. Stay within the stated generic contract rather than using raw types to suppress errors.

blocks.title: Contracts are better than guesses
paragraphs: Preserve behavior when refactoring, treat input grammar as data, and let generic types reject invalid combinations. Scope, API contracts and tests matter more than style metrics by themselves.

cards.prompt: Why extract parsing from a method that reads console input and prints results?
cards.answer: A pure parsing boundary can be tested with supplied text, reused by file input, and report a clear failure without owning UI behavior. The split should follow responsibilities, not an arbitrary line count.

cards.prompt: Does high line coverage prove a refactoring is correct?
cards.answer: No. Executed lines may have weak assertions or miss meaningful inputs. Preserve behavior with requirement-based assertions and boundary/failure cases.

cards.prompt: Why can split(regex, -1) matter for validating delimited records?
cards.answer: It preserves trailing empty fields, so a missing final value can be detected. Also remember that the delimiter is a regular expression and may need escaping.

cards.prompt: Does calling text.trim() change the String referenced by text?
cards.answer: No. String is immutable; trim returns a result. Use that returned value deliberately, and do not silently trim where the format treats whitespace as meaningful.

cards.prompt: Why can a List<String> not be assigned to List<Object>?
cards.answer: The wider reference would allow inserting a non-String Object into the same list. Java rejects that assignment to preserve the String element contract.

cards.prompt: Does type erasure make a raw collection as safe as a parameterized collection?
cards.answer: No. Parameterized types provide compile-time checks and typed access; erasure does not justify bypassing them. Raw operations can postpone failures to runtime casts.

guided.title: Review a delimiter parser
guided.prompt: A format has exactly three fields separated by #, including an optional final comment. Empty comments are valid; missing separators are invalid. A candidate uses split("#"), indexes all three fields immediately and catches every exception to return a default record.
rubric: The parser preserves an empty trailing field and checks field count before indexing.
Malformed input is reported according to the contract, not converted into fictional data.
Tests distinguish missing separators, empty allowed comment, too many fields and numeric conversion failures if relevant.
reference: Use split("#", -1) and require exactly three fields. This accepts "name#4#" while rejecting "name#4". Validate each nonoptional field under its own rule.
Keep parsing separate from reading/printing and expose a meaningful failure. Multiple small implementations can satisfy the format without matching one reference text.
